standard.title: Protective Behaviours and Help-Seeking
standard.description: demonstrate protective behaviours, name body parts and rehearse help-seeking strategies that help keep them safe
standard.prior_knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students have some awareness of trusted adults from home and care settings. No prior structured curriculum work on protective behaviours, anatomical naming or assertive help-seeking.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students demonstrate protective behaviours, name body parts correctly, and rehearse help-seeking strategies including identifying trusted adults and assertive strategies for unsafe situations.

nodes.label: Naming body parts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can name body parts using correct anatomical language, and understand that all people have the right to bodily autonomy.
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least the major external body parts including private body parts using correct anatomical terms.
nodes.typical_width: Name a full range of body parts using correct anatomical language; discuss why using correct names is important; articulate that all people have the right to bodily autonomy — the right to make choices about what others ask them to do with their bodies.
wider: Explore body-naming in different health and safety contexts — swimming, first aid — where correct naming matters
Discuss the difference between public and private body parts and why privacy rules exist
Connect anatomical naming to protective behaviours — being able to describe accurately when something has happened
nodes.hinge_reason: Correct anatomical language is prerequisite for describing unsafe situations clearly to trusted adults. Students who cannot name body parts accurately cannot effectively communicate when protective behaviours have been violated.

response_modes.reason: Anatomical naming requires straightforward, repeated, normalised practice to overcome social awkwardness. Matter-of-fact lesson delivery and consistent correct language are the key teaching moves.

success_criteria: Names major body parts including private body parts using correct anatomical terms
States that their body belongs to them and that others must ask before touching

nodes.label: Trusted adults and support networks
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify a support network of trusted adults they can go to if they feel unsafe, uncomfortable or scared.
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least two trusted adults they could go to for help if they felt unsafe.
nodes.typical_width: Identify a support network of trusted adults including family, school and community figures; explain what makes someone a trusted adult; distinguish between comfortable and uncomfortable situations that need trusted adult support.
wider: Discuss what makes an adult trustworthy and how to judge who is safe to go to
Explore trusted adult networks in different community contexts, including in First Nations Australian family and community structures
Identify trusted online spaces and digital tools, and discuss when to seek help from a trusted adult if feeling unsafe online
nodes.hinge_reason: Knowing who to go to is prerequisite for all help-seeking strategies (next node). Without a concrete trusted adult support network, help-seeking strategies are abstract and unusable. This is one of the highest-stakes cascade risks in the Foundation band.

response_modes.reason: Trusted adult networks vary by context — at school, at home, in community, online. Discuss each context so students know who their trusted adults are across settings, not only at school.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Community, cultural and online contexts for trusted adult identification are pedagogically significant — they prepare students for real-world help-seeking beyond the classroom.
success_criteria: Names at least two trusted adults who could help them if they felt unsafe
Describes at least one situation that would require them to go to a trusted adult

nodes.label: Protective behaviours and assertive help-seeking
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore and demonstrate protective behaviours and assertive strategies for seeking help when they or others feel unsafe or uncomfortable.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate at least one assertive strategy for seeking help in an unsafe situation (e.g. saying 'no', moving away, telling a trusted adult).
nodes.typical_width: Explore and demonstrate a range of protective behaviours and assertive help-seeking strategies; practise responses to unsafe or uncomfortable scenarios; rehearse help-seeking with trusted adults.
wider: Rehearse help-seeking in varied scenarios — physical, emotional and online unsafe situations
Practise assertive strategies with different trusted adults in different contexts
Explore how to help a friend who is unsafe, extending help-seeking beyond self-protection

response_modes.reason: Protective behaviours and help-seeking require rehearsal — not just knowledge. Foundation students need repeated, low-stakes role-play scenarios where they practise the actual words and actions of help-seeking.

success_criteria: Demonstrates at least one assertive protective behaviour (saying no, moving away, telling a trusted adult)
Rehearses a help-seeking response in a scenario involving an unsafe or uncomfortable situation
